headline: Trump warns Iran of fresh offensive if no deal reached
description: US president says war will end ‘very soon’ either through diplomacy or military action
author: Web Desk
article_text:
US President Donald Trump has warned that Iran could face another major military offensive if it fails to reach a deal with Washington, while insisting the conflict would end “very soon”, either through diplomacy or further military action.

Speaking to Right Side Broadcasting Network before a campaign rally in Iowa on Sunday, Trump said the United States had achieved a major victory and would soon bring the war to an end.

“We’ve had such a victory, and we’ll put it away very soon, one way or the other. Either they’ll make a deal, or we’ll just end it,” he said.

Addressing supporters ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections, Trump said he wanted to avoid further loss of life but warned that Washington could eventually have to deliver a decisive military blow to Tehran.

“The only reason we are not finished with Iran is because I want to be nice. I want to try and save all those lives if I can. But at some point, we’re going to have to give them the hammer,” he said.

Trump also defended rising oil prices amid the conflict, describing them as a small price to pay for security and predicting that energy prices would fall sharply once the fighting ended.

He reiterated that the US military campaign had prevented Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons and warned that additional Iranian nuclear facilities, including the suspected underground installation known as Pickaxe Mountain, could be targeted.

Despite the threats, Trump said diplomatic efforts were progressing, although he questioned Tehran’s reliability in negotiations.

Indirect talks between Washington and Tehran continued under Qatari mediation, with reports suggesting preliminary understandings had been reached on Iran’s nuclear programme, maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz and possible economic incentives for Tehran.

Earlier on Sunday, Iran’s top diplomat said he hoped Washington would act with “rationality” as diplomatic efforts continued to avert a return to full-scale war.

headline: Nine people dead in Learjet crash in south Florida, officials say
description: Aircraft was heading to Bahamas when it crashed in a residential area, prompting an evacuation
author: Reuters
article_text:
A Learjet crashed on Sunday afternoon in a residential area in Palm Beach County, Florida, ‌killing all nine people on board, US transportation officials said.

The private jet had taken off from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was headed to North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas, the Federal Aviation Administration said in a statement.

Videos on social ​media showed the jet slamming into the ground next to a road and exploding.

“It was a ​big-time tragedy that happened,” Florida Governor Ron DeSantis said at a press conference near ⁠the crash site in Lake Worth Beach.

“When you see that video, it’s a jarring thing. It was like ​a missile coming down, and a massive explosion, debris going everywhere.”

The National Transportation Safety Board said it had ​launched an investigation into the crash, which Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called a “horrific tragedy.”

FAA records list the Bombardier-made Learjet 60’s owner as a Delaware corporation.

Canada-based Bombardier said it would fully support the investigation and cooperate as needed.

The crash left a “massive crater” ​by the road near the entrance to a mobile home park, Palm Beach County Commissioner Joel Flores ​said at the news conference. About 600 people were being evacuated from the area and relocated to two shelters in the ‌county, ⁠Flores said.

Heavy rainfall and thunderstorms were occurring in the area at the time, forecaster AccuWeather said in a statement.

An audio recording from a Miami air traffic control centre posted on LiveATC, a site that broadcasts air traffic control communications, captured the plane’s final moments before the crash in unusual detail.

At first, someone in the plane’s ​cockpit reported to an ​air traffic controller that ⁠they were “managing the ice” but faced “moderate” turbulence and were seeking “better rides”.

Less than a minute later, the person said “Mayday, mayday,” reporting that the plane was suddenly descending at a ​rate of 10,000 feet per minute.

Seconds later, the person said they were declaring ​an emergency, ⁠with the rate of descent accelerating to 20,000 feet per minute.

Less than 20 seconds later, the person said: “We’re going to crash into the ground” before saying that the descent rate had reached 22,000 feet per minute as the ⁠plane started ​banking.

About 35 seconds after the initial mayday announcement, the last thing ​heard from the cockpit was a rapidly spoken “We’re out of time.”

Flight tracking website Flightradar24 said data showed the vertical descent rate at ​one point exceeded 32,000 feet per minute.

headline: Michigan Democrat backs Republican in key US Senate race
description: Haley Stevens endorses Mike Rogers after losing her party’s primary to Abdul El Sayed
author: Reuters
article_text:
A prominent Michigan Democrat endorsed Republican Mike Rogers on Sunday, giving President Donald Trump’s Republicans an unexpected boost in ​a critical US Senate race two days before midterm elections that will decide control of Congress.

US Representative Haley Stevens, who lost the Michigan Democrats’ Senate primary to Abdul El Sayed in a bitterly ‌contested race, publicly backed Rogers and appeared with him at a Detroit church, threatening to worsen divisions in a state viewed as crucial to Democratic hopes of retaking the US Senate.

“I don’t belong in Abdul’s campaign,” Stevens said in a video posted to social media.

Hours later at a political rally in Iowa, Trump invited Stevens to join the Republican Party.

He told reporters beforehand that he would reach out to her to thank her for the endorsement, which he called “a smart thing to do because El Sayed would destroy our country.”

Thirty-five Senate seats and ​all 435 House of Representatives seats are on the ballot on Tuesday.

Republicans hold narrow majorities in both chambers. Polls show Democrats are favoured to win a majority of the House and are locked in a ​tight battle for control of the Senate, where the outcome likely will rest with a handful of states, including Michigan and Alaska.

If Democrats take control of the House or ⁠Senate, they could block Trump’s legislative agenda for his final two years in office and launch investigations of an administration that has so far faced largely compliant Republican majorities.

The White House has been preparing to implement portions of Trump’s agenda ​without the aid of Congress, including its tariff pressure on trading partners.

Michigan rift

Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers came on the day she was scheduled to appear with El Sayed in a show of party unity.

But the planned event unravelled after Stevens called ​on El Sayed to condemn an outside group’s ad that she said blames Israel for high grocery prices.

“That ad was very painful,” Stevens told CNN on Sunday night.

“There are so many Democrats who want to vote for our Democratic nominee, and they’re just being told, ‘Hey, this is a party you don’t belong in, or this is a campaign you don’t belong in.’”

El Sayed’s campaign recently asked Stevens to skip his events through Election Day so as “not to distract from the central issues of the campaign,” a person familiar with the matter said.

Republicans sought to capitalise ​on Stevens’ move.

“This is courage in politics in America today,” Rogers said.

“When you see a party, and at least a sliver of the party, veering off into the virulent hate that they have been spewing toward a group of ​people, it gets dangerous.”

Later on Sunday at the Iowa rally, Trump repeated false claims that El Sayed is a “jihadist” — attacks that fit a broader pattern of inflammatory rhetoric from Trump and other Republicans targeting Arab Americans and Muslims.

Stevens’ move did not appear to dent support ‌for El Sayed. A ⁠New York Times/Siena poll released and partly conducted on Sunday showed the Democratic nominee with a 53% to 42% lead over Rogers.

A spokesperson for El Sayed’s campaign said that it raised $1.2 million in the four hours after Stevens endorsed Rogers, making it the campaign’s second-best fundraising day since the Democratic primary election in August.

He declined to address Stevens’ endorsement on Sunday directly.

“This race was never about me,” El Sayed told MS NOW. “It was never even about Mike Rogers. It’s certainly not about Haley Stevens. This race is about the people in the state of Michigan, the people that I’ve gotten to know in their churches and synagogues, in their basements and their living rooms, talking about what they need and deserve.”

Several ​of Stevens’ congressional staff resigned over the endorsement, according to ​reports from CNN and the Hill, while some voters expressed ⁠disdain.

“Haley Stevens is a traitor,” said Pamela Johnson, 72, after voting for El Sayed in Warren, a Detroit suburb.

article_html:
A prominent Michigan Democrat endorsed Republican Mike Rogers on Sunday, giving President Donald Trump’s Republicans an unexpected boost in ​a critical US Senate race two days before midterm elections that will decide control of Congress.

US Representative Haley Stevens, who lost the Michigan Democrats’ Senate primary to Abdul El Sayed in a bitterly ‌contested race, publicly backed Rogers and appeared with him at a Detroit church, threatening to worsen divisions in a state viewed as crucial to Democratic hopes of retaking the US Senate.

“I don’t belong in Abdul’s campaign,” Stevens said in a video posted to social media.

Hours later at a political rally in Iowa, Trump invited Stevens to join the Republican Party.

He told reporters beforehand that he would reach out to her to thank her for the endorsement, which he called “a smart thing to do because El Sayed would destroy our country.”

Thirty-five Senate seats and ​all 435 House of Representatives seats are on the ballot on Tuesday.

Republicans hold narrow majorities in both chambers. Polls show Democrats are favoured to win a majority of the House and are locked in a ​tight battle for control of the Senate, where the outcome likely will rest with a handful of states, including Michigan and Alaska.

If Democrats take control of the House or ⁠Senate, they could block Trump’s legislative agenda for his final two years in office and launch investigations of an administration that has so far faced largely compliant Republican majorities.

The White House has been preparing to implement portions of Trump’s agenda ​without the aid of Congress, including its tariff pressure on trading partners.

Michigan rift

Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers came on the day she was scheduled to appear with El Sayed in a show of party unity.

But the planned event unravelled after Stevens called ​on El Sayed to condemn an outside group’s ad that she said blames Israel for high grocery prices.

“That ad was very painful,” Stevens told CNN on Sunday night.

“There are so many Democrats who want to vote for our Democratic nominee, and they’re just being told, ‘Hey, this is a party you don’t belong in, or this is a campaign you don’t belong in.’”

El Sayed’s campaign recently asked Stevens to skip his events through Election Day so as “not to distract from the central issues of the campaign,” a person familiar with the matter said.

Republicans sought to capitalise ​on Stevens’ move.

“This is courage in politics in America today,” Rogers said.

“When you see a party, and at least a sliver of the party, veering off into the virulent hate that they have been spewing toward a group of ​people, it gets dangerous.”

Later on Sunday at the Iowa rally, Trump repeated false claims that El Sayed is a “jihadist” — attacks that fit a broader pattern of inflammatory rhetoric from Trump and other Republicans targeting Arab Americans and Muslims.

Stevens’ move did not appear to dent support ‌for El Sayed. A ⁠New York Times/Siena poll released and partly conducted on Sunday showed the Democratic nominee with a 53% to 42% lead over Rogers.

A spokesperson for El Sayed’s campaign said that it raised $1.2 million in the four hours after Stevens endorsed Rogers, making it the campaign’s second-best fundraising day since the Democratic primary election in August.

He declined to address Stevens’ endorsement on Sunday directly.

“This race was never about me,” El Sayed told MS NOW. “It was never even about Mike Rogers. It’s certainly not about Haley Stevens. This race is about the people in the state of Michigan, the people that I’ve gotten to know in their churches and synagogues, in their basements and their living rooms, talking about what they need and deserve.”

Several ​of Stevens’ congressional staff resigned over the endorsement, according to ​reports from CNN and the Hill, while some voters expressed ⁠disdain.

“Haley Stevens is a traitor,” said Pamela Johnson, 72, after voting for El Sayed in Warren, a Detroit suburb.

headline: Crew from NASA's simulated Mars mission emerges after 378 days in isolation
description: Four crew members complete 378 days in isolation as part of NASA’s simulated Mars mission
author: Reuters
article_text:
The four members of a crew who took part in a simulated mission to Mars have emerged after 378 days in isolation ​at the US space agency’s Johnson Space Centre in Houston, an endeavour designed to help prepare for a ‌possible future excursion by NASA astronauts to Earth’s planetary neighbour.

“It’s been a hell of a year — analogue astronauts living in captivity of our own free will,” Ellen Ellis, the medical officer on the Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analogue, or CHAPEA, mission, said in remarks at Johnson Space Centre after ​emerging with her three crewmates on Saturday.

The four entered the 1,700-square-foot 3D-printed habitat on October 19, 2025, and performed ​tasks such as growing crops in simulated Martian soil and interfacing with NASA officials with delays ⁠recreating those inherent in interplanetary communications.

NASA, which has explored Mars with robotic rovers and orbiting spacecraft, has ambitions for a human mission ​to Mars as early as the 2030s, with plans before that to return astronauts to the Moon for the first time since 1972.

“We ​have a narrowing window of opportunity to maintain US preeminence in space,” Ellis said.

Ellis mentioned the service academy for space-related operations pursued by President Donald Trump’s administration and plans for a lunar base.

“Let’s seize the initiative, lead with science that will benefit our economy and ensure our legacy in space for our ​children’s children,” Ellis said.

The other crew members were mission commander Ross Elder, science officer Matthew Montgomery and flight engineer James Spicer.

“For ​Mars, the risks are great,” Elder said in remarks after emerging from isolation.

“But through seeking understanding, strong vision and leadership, creativity, fortitude, hard work ‌and an incredible foundation, the goal of putting humans on Mars is not only achievable, but rather inevitable.”

The crew is set to participate in two weeks of post-mission evaluations and debriefing with NASA scientists.

NASA has said it is looking for insight into what it takes for astronauts to adapt to the routines and demands of daily life on long-duration missions beyond Earth to keep them healthy, productive, ​and connected.

This was NASA’s second ​CHAPEA mission, with another four-person ⁠crew in isolation at Johnson Space Centre for 378 days spanning 2023 and 2024.

Vanessa Wyche, director of the Johnson Space Centre, greeted the crew members when they exited isolation.

Wyche said they ​managed to live with limited resources, maintain their habitat, and carry out simulated Mars operations.

Wyche also ​noted how the ⁠crew dealt with the simulated interplanetary communications, with lag times between sending messages and receiving responses.

“These delays require patience, careful planning and greater independence — qualities that will be essential for future astronauts travelling millions of miles from home,” Wyche said.

Wyche said the lessons learned from ⁠the CHAPEA ​crew and their experiences will help pave the way for the missions first ​to the Moon and “one day, Mars.”

“But through seeking understanding, strong vision and leadership, creativity, fortitude, hard work ‌and an incredible foundation, the goal of putting humans on Mars is not only achievable, but rather inevitable.”
The crew is set to participate in two weeks of post-mission evaluations and debriefing with NASA scientists.

NASA has said it is looking for insight into what it takes for astronauts to adapt to the routines and demands of daily life on long-duration missions beyond Earth to keep them healthy, productive, and connected.
This was NASA’s second CHAPEA mission, with another four-person ⁠crew in isolation at Johnson Space Centre for 378 days spanning 2023 and 2024.
Vanessa Wyche, director of the Johnson Space Centre, greeted the crew members when they exited isolation.
Wyche said they managed to live with limited resources, maintain their habitat, and carry out simulated Mars operations.
Wyche also noted how the ⁠crew dealt with the simulated interplanetary communications, with lag times between sending messages and receiving responses.
“These delays require patience, careful planning and greater independence — qualities that will be essential for future astronauts travelling millions of miles from home,” Wyche said.
Wyche said the lessons learned from ⁠the CHAPEA crew and their experiences will help pave the way for the missions first to the Moon and “one day, Mars.”

headline: Netanyahu urges Trump to strike Iran after US midterms: Report
description: US president favours allowing negotiations with Tehran to continue, Axios reports
author: Web Desk
article_text:
US President Donald Trump spoke with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu about whether and when to intensify military operations against Iran, US media reported on Sunday.

Axios, citing one US and one Israeli official, reported that the two leaders discussed the state of negotiations with Tehran, with Netanyahu urging Trump to launch strikes immediately after the US midterm elections, while the US president favoured allowing diplomacy to continue.

The Israeli official described the call as “tough”, while the US official called it “direct”, according to the report.

Throughout the eight-month war, Trump has pursued both military action and negotiations with Iran, seeking a deal that could pave the way for peace talks and fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz to vital oil and gas traffic.

On Saturday, Trump told reporters that negotiations with Tehran were “going fine” and said there were still one or two targets to “take care of”.

He also said Washington was in no hurry to launch further offensive operations, arguing that US strikes had already severely damaged Iran’s military and nuclear programme.

Trump has faced mounting domestic pressure over the war, as rising petrol prices and other living costs fuel voter discontent ahead of the US midterm elections.

The economic fallout could pose a challenge for Republicans as voters prepare to decide control of Congress.

headline: Oil prices ease 3% on optimism for Qatari-led talks on ending Iran war
description: Brent crude falls to $109.75 a barrel as Iranian and Qatari officials continue talks to end conflict
author: Reuters
article_text:
Oil prices slipped more than 3% on Monday after Iranian and Qatari officials ‌held a third straight day of talks aimed at pushing for a deal to end the US-Israeli war on Iran.

Brent crude futures fell $3.68, or 3.2%, to $109.75 a barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate crude ​was at $100.69 a barrel, down $3.43, or 3.3%.

Brent ended October at its highest in six ​months amid concerns that the US-Iran conflict could escalate again after Tuesday’s US midterm ⁠elections.

“Oil is seeing a technical pullback this morning after last week’s strong gains,” said Tim ​Waterer, chief market analyst at KCM Trade.

“Lingering hopes of some form of diplomatic progress, combined with ​the absence of any meaningful military escalation over the weekend, have taken some of the immediate heat out of prices for now.”

However, the market remained alert to the possibility that rhetoric around Iran could be ratcheted ​higher and push Brent toward $120 after the midterm elections, Waterer said.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said ​on Sunday that the purpose of the “ongoing and progressing” talks was to continue consultations with the Qatari mediators, ‌adding ⁠Tehran was prepared for “both defence and diplomacy”.

The talks come amid attacks on oil tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz that are driving up global energy and shipping costs.

In October, Saudi Arabia increased crude exports versus September despite attacks by the Iran-aligned Yemeni Houthis on its energy infrastructure, two of ​three ship-tracking companies said.

“The ​price action in ⁠oil in recent weeks reflects a market increasingly bracing for the potential for more hostilities between the US and Iran,” ING analysts said in ​a client note.

“If the midterms pass with neither strikes nor a deal, ​the key ⁠question is whether the market continues to price in a substantial geopolitical risk premium or whether that premium gradually begins to unwind.”

The Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies, including Russia, or ⁠OPEC+, kept December ​production targets steady on Sunday, confirming expectations that more ​policy adjustments will not occur until next year, as the group continues to struggle with export disruptions from the Iran ​war.

headline: India evacuates thousands ahead of second cyclone in a week
description: Authorities plan to move 30,000 people as Cyclone Murasu approaches southeastern coast
author: Reuters
article_text:
Authorities began evacuating people along India’s eastern ​coast on Monday, a day before ‌a severe cyclonic storm is expected to make landfall in a region recovering from a deadly ​cyclone last week.

Cyclone Murasu is ​expected to be less intense than ⁠last week’s cyclone Arnab, where six ​people were killed, and dozens of houses ​and crops were destroyed.

India Meteorological Department (IMD) has forecast Murasu to make landfall in the early ​hours of Tuesday.

“Around 2,000 people have ​been evacuated, and the process is continuing. We are ‌planning ⁠to evacuate some 30,000 people,” Prakhar Jain, managing director of the Andhra Pradesh State Disaster Management Authority, told Reuters ​on Monday.

The ​cyclone ⁠formed over the Bay of Bengal, a major region for ​tropical cyclones that has spawned ​deadly ⁠storms on India’s east coast.

IMD expects Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh, states along ⁠India’s southeastern coast, to ​feel the brunt of it.

headline: Trump White House prepares to govern without Congress if Democrats win
description: Administration officials draw up plans to advance Trump agenda through executive powers
author: Reuters
article_text:
US President Donald Trump’s White House has spent months preparing for a possible Democratic takeover of Congress, developing plans to keep advancing major parts of his agenda through executive power while bracing for ​investigations of his administration, according to a White House official and two people familiar with the plans.

Senior officials, including deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller and budget director Russell Vought, have been working with the ‌White House Counsel’s Office since April to identify executive actions on immigration, tariffs, housing costs and federal spending that Trump could pursue without congressional approval, said the three people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

White House counsel Will Scharf and his team also are looking at “what Trump can legally do on his own, where he could push the limits of his authority and how to defend those decisions in court,” the White House official said.

The planning underscores a paradox of Tuesday’s midterm elections: Capturing control of Congress would give Democrats the power to investigate Trump, block legislation and ​constrain his spending priorities.

But Trump would retain broad executive authority over trade, foreign policy and the federal bureaucracy that he has already used aggressively during his second term.

If Republicans lose control of Congress, Trump said he expects he ​could issue vetoes for “a month or two” before reaching compromises with Democrats.

“I guess I’ll become Mr Veto,” Trump told the New York Post‘s Pod Force One podcast in an interview excerpt ⁠released on Sunday. “And then at some point, we’ll probably make deals.“

Democrats need a net gain of four seats in the US House of Representatives as well as the US Senate to overturn Republicans’ narrow 218-214 and 53-47 majorities.

Opinion polls favour Democrats ​to win the House, while the Senate remains too close to call.

For the past month, Trump has held rallies across the country trying to preserve Republican control of Congress, even as his aides privately prepare for a very different political landscape in 2027.

The ​White House pushed back on the prospect of Republican losses and accused the media of promoting a false narrative.

“This administration and commonsense Republicans will continue to secure our borders, restore law and order, putting more money back into the pockets of hard-working Americans, and deliver wins for the American people,” White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said.

Among the executive actions under consideration are new tariffs on imports of critical minerals and wind turbines, tighter rules on visas for international students and temporary foreign workers, and measures aimed at lowering housing and construction costs, the White House official said.

Federal agencies ​have submitted proposals and legal reviews of actions the administration could take unilaterally, one of the people with knowledge of the plans said.

Vought, whose US Office of Management and Budget oversees federal spending, is examining which priorities can move forward using money ​already appropriated by Congress, two of the people said.

He also wants to change federal grant rules to give political appointees more say in which government programmes receive taxpayer money, they said, potentially giving the White House more influence over federal spending without seeking congressional approval.

Trump has been ‌briefed on the ⁠preparations and has taken part in discussions about them, the White House official said.

When asked how comfortable Trump would be governing through executive authority under a Democratic Congress, one of the people said, “very comfortable.”

Governing without Congress

Trump has already tested the reach of presidential power since returning to office in January 2025, using executive authority to impose sweeping tariffs, intensify immigration enforcement, shrink the federal workforce, and pursue foreign-policy goals including the war against Iran without Congress’ approval or new laws.

A major exception was Trump’s massive package of tax and spending cuts that was passed by the Republican-controlled Congress and signed into law by the president in July 2025.

“President Trump in the last two years has basically ignored Congress and tried to do as much as possible through executive orders and ​executive power,” said Nathan Gonzales, editor at Inside Elections, which provides ​nonpartisan political analysis.

“I think he will only continue if ⁠there are Democratic majorities.”

Trump has repeatedly invoked national emergencies to expand his ability to act without new legislation.

Congress can vote to end those emergencies, but Trump could veto such a move, requiring two-thirds majorities in both chambers to override him.

A Democratic Congress could still create significant obstacles.

article_html:
US President Donald Trump’s White House has spent months preparing for a possible Democratic takeover of Congress, developing plans to keep advancing major parts of his agenda through executive power while bracing for ​investigations of his administration, according to a White House official and two people familiar with the plans.

Senior officials, including deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller and budget director Russell Vought, have been working with the ‌White House Counsel’s Office since April to identify executive actions on immigration, tariffs, housing costs and federal spending that Trump could pursue without congressional approval, said the three people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

White House counsel Will Scharf and his team also are looking at “what Trump can legally do on his own, where he could push the limits of his authority and how to defend those decisions in court,” the White House official said.

The planning underscores a paradox of Tuesday’s midterm elections: Capturing control of Congress would give Democrats the power to investigate Trump, block legislation and ​constrain his spending priorities.

But Trump would retain broad executive authority over trade, foreign policy and the federal bureaucracy that he has already used aggressively during his second term.

If Republicans lose control of Congress, Trump said he expects he ​could issue vetoes for “a month or two” before reaching compromises with Democrats.

“I guess I’ll become Mr Veto,” Trump told the New York Post‘s Pod Force One podcast in an interview excerpt ⁠released on Sunday. “And then at some point, we’ll probably make deals.“

Democrats need a net gain of four seats in the US House of Representatives as well as the US Senate to overturn Republicans’ narrow 218-214 and 53-47 majorities.

Opinion polls favour Democrats ​to win the House, while the Senate remains too close to call.

For the past month, Trump has held rallies across the country trying to preserve Republican control of Congress, even as his aides privately prepare for a very different political landscape in 2027.

The ​White House pushed back on the prospect of Republican losses and accused the media of promoting a false narrative.

“This administration and commonsense Republicans will continue to secure our borders, restore law and order, putting more money back into the pockets of hard-working Americans, and deliver wins for the American people,” White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said.

Among the executive actions under consideration are new tariffs on imports of critical minerals and wind turbines, tighter rules on visas for international students and temporary foreign workers, and measures aimed at lowering housing and construction costs, the White House official said.

Federal agencies ​have submitted proposals and legal reviews of actions the administration could take unilaterally, one of the people with knowledge of the plans said.

Vought, whose US Office of Management and Budget oversees federal spending, is examining which priorities can move forward using money ​already appropriated by Congress, two of the people said.

He also wants to change federal grant rules to give political appointees more say in which government programmes receive taxpayer money, they said, potentially giving the White House more influence over federal spending without seeking congressional approval.

Trump has been ‌briefed on the ⁠preparations and has taken part in discussions about them, the White House official said.

When asked how comfortable Trump would be governing through executive authority under a Democratic Congress, one of the people said, “very comfortable.”

Governing without Congress

Trump has already tested the reach of presidential power since returning to office in January 2025, using executive authority to impose sweeping tariffs, intensify immigration enforcement, shrink the federal workforce, and pursue foreign-policy goals including the war against Iran without Congress’ approval or new laws.

A major exception was Trump’s massive package of tax and spending cuts that was passed by the Republican-controlled Congress and signed into law by the president in July 2025.

“President Trump in the last two years has basically ignored Congress and tried to do as much as possible through executive orders and ​executive power,” said Nathan Gonzales, editor at Inside Elections, which provides ​nonpartisan political analysis.

“I think he will only continue if ⁠there are Democratic majorities.”

Trump has repeatedly invoked national emergencies to expand his ability to act without new legislation.

Congress can vote to end those emergencies, but Trump could veto such a move, requiring two-thirds majorities in both chambers to override him.

A Democratic Congress could still create significant obstacles.

Control of the Senate would allow Democrats to block Trump’s judicial and executive-branch nominees, including any Supreme ​Court pick.

“I would anticipate they will be very reluctant to approve any of the president’s appointments,” said Andrew Busch, a public policy professor at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, and ​author of a history of midterm ⁠elections.

Democrats could also refuse to pass Trump-backed legislation. But Trump could veto Democratic legislation he doesn’t like, and Democrats are unlikely to have enough votes in the House to override him.

Courts could block executive actions that exceed Trump’s legal authority.

The White House plans to seek legal opinions from the Justice Department to determine what Trump can do without Congress and how to defend those actions if they are challenged in court, one of the people said.

Democratic investigations

One challenge, however, cannot be sidestepped through executive action: congressional investigations.

Reuters previously reported that senior House ⁠Democrats and committee ​aides have discussed using hearings, subpoenas and document requests to examine whether Trump has used his presidential power to benefit himself, allies or donors.

Trump aides ​have been preparing for that prospect for months, all three people said.

White House lawyers have been briefing political appointees and agency leaders on how to handle congressional inquiries, document requests and subpoenas, one person said.

They have advised officials to be careful about what they put in writing.

They also sought a Justice Department ​opinion that could allow Trump to invoke executive privilege to shield communications with private advisers from congressional scrutiny, the person said.

headline: Democrats open 7-point lead in race for control of Congress: Poll
description: Trump's disapproval rating at 60%, three-quarters of voters unhappy with his handling of economy
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Democrats hold a seven-point lead over Republicans in the race for control of Congress ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, as growing dissatisfaction with President Donald Trump and the US economy weighs on his party, according to a new NBC News poll.

The survey, conducted among registered voters from October 28 to 30, found that 52% favoured a Democratic-controlled Congress, compared with 45% who preferred Republican control.

According to the survey, Democrats managed a 21-point lead among independents. About 3% of respondents remained undecided.

The survey showed that 60% of voters disapproved of Trump’s performance, while 40% approved of his presidency.

It also found that around three-quarters of voters were unhappy with his handling of the economy, while 64% said he had failed to live up to their expectations.

Seven in 10 said the country was heading in the wrong direction.

Inflation and the cost of living ranked as voters’ top concerns, followed by government corruption, threats to democracy, and immigration and border security.

Democrats held a slight advantage on handling inflation, while Republicans led by just two points on the broader economy, a significant decline from their double-digit advantage in recent years.

The poll also found growing discontent among Republicans, with 53% dissatisfied with the economy and 37% saying Trump had failed to meet his promises.

Although his approval remained high at 93% among Republicans identifying with the MAGA movement, it fell to 54% among non-MAGA Republicans.

Despite their national lead, Democrats face obstacles. Only 29% of voters viewed the party positively, compared with 38% for Republicans, suggesting their advantage is driven more by opposition to the GOP than strong support for Democrats.

Republicans also retained leads in their own districts and in states Trump won in 2024 — areas that will be crucial to the battle for both chambers of Congress.

Democrats need to regain Republican-held ground to take control of Congress, including at least two states Trump carried by double-digit margins to win the Senate.

The survey also found Republicans narrowly ahead on handling government corruption, while both parties’ congressional leaders received relatively poor public ratings.

The poll was conducted by Democratic pollster Jeff Horwitt of Hart Research Associates and Republican pollster Bill McInturff of Public Opinion Strategies.

The findings suggest Democrats have a national advantage heading into the midterms, but their ability to turn it into a congressional majority remains uncertain.

article_html:
Democrats hold a seven-point lead over Republicans in the race for control of Congress ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, as growing dissatisfaction with President Donald Trump and the US economy weighs on his party, according to a new NBC News poll.

The survey, conducted among registered voters from October 28 to 30, found that 52% favoured a Democratic-controlled Congress, compared with 45% who preferred Republican control.

According to the survey, Democrats managed a 21-point lead among independents. About 3% of respondents remained undecided.

The survey showed that 60% of voters disapproved of Trump’s performance, while 40% approved of his presidency.

It also found that around three-quarters of voters were unhappy with his handling of the economy, while 64% said he had failed to live up to their expectations.

Seven in 10 said the country was heading in the wrong direction.

Inflation and the cost of living ranked as voters’ top concerns, followed by government corruption, threats to democracy, and immigration and border security.

Democrats held a slight advantage on handling inflation, while Republicans led by just two points on the broader economy, a significant decline from their double-digit advantage in recent years.

The poll also found growing discontent among Republicans, with 53% dissatisfied with the economy and 37% saying Trump had failed to meet his promises.

Although his approval remained high at 93% among Republicans identifying with the MAGA movement, it fell to 54% among non-MAGA Republicans.

Despite their national lead, Democrats face obstacles. Only 29% of voters viewed the party positively, compared with 38% for Republicans, suggesting their advantage is driven more by opposition to the GOP than strong support for Democrats.

Republicans also retained leads in their own districts and in states Trump won in 2024 — areas that will be crucial to the battle for both chambers of Congress.

Democrats need to regain Republican-held ground to take control of Congress, including at least two states Trump carried by double-digit margins to win the Senate.

The survey also found Republicans narrowly ahead on handling government corruption, while both parties’ congressional leaders received relatively poor public ratings.

The poll was conducted by Democratic pollster Jeff Horwitt of Hart Research Associates and Republican pollster Bill McInturff of Public Opinion Strategies.

The findings suggest Democrats have a national advantage heading into the midterms, but their ability to turn it into a congressional majority remains uncertain.

headline: Kimi Antonelli becomes youngest Formula One world champion at 20
description: Mercedes driver clinches title with a third-place finish at the Mexico City Grand Prix
author: Reuters
article_text:
A tearful Kimi Antonelli became Formula One’s youngest world champion at 20 years and 68 days old on Sunday when he finished third for Mercedes in a red-flagged and restarted ​Mexico City Grand Prix won by Red Bull’s Max Verstappen.

The first Italian champion since 1953 sobbed with joy over the team radio as he took the chequered flag at the high-altitude ‌Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez, with his overall lead now an unassailable 119 points.

Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton started from pole position and took a close second place – after clashing with teammate Charles Leclerc – on an afternoon of drama with two safety cars, multiple crashes and an agonising 33-minute halt with 25 of the 71 laps remaining.

“Get in there, Kimi. Champion of the world,” said his race engineer Peter Bonnington, a regular target for the young driver’s practical jokes.

“We did it, thank you so much,” gasped the Italian, whose parents and sister ​were there to embrace him when he stepped out of the car. He was then mobbed by his pit crew.

The previous youngest champion was Germany’s Sebastian Vettel, who took the first of his four ​with Red Bull at 23 years and 134 days in 2010.

“I’m speechless. I’m trying to process what has just happened,” said Antonelli in comments to the crowd.

“It’s ⁠been an incredible season, and to share this podium with Max and Lewis is truly incredible. And looking forward to some more battles in the future.

“This weekend I did feel a bit more tense, but I’m just ​so happy that we got it done, and now we can enjoy the rest of the season,” he added, with an Italian flag wrapped around his shoulders on the podium and spraying the champagne with abandon.

The last Italian champion ​was Alberto Ascari, 73 years earlier.

“On the last lap, I just backed off because I just couldn’t see the track. I was getting emotional,” Antonelli told a later news conference.

“So it was just good to bring it home.”

Verstappen goes second overall

Leclerc finished fourth, McLaren’s outgoing champion Lando Norris was fifth and Antonelli’s teammate George Russell only sixth in a race he had to win to have any chance of staying in contention.

That also meant Verstappen went second in the overall standings, with Hamilton third and pre-season ​favourite Russell plummeting to fourth and 130 points behind Antonelli.

Mercedes have 630 points in the constructors’ standings to Ferrari’s 504 and could clinch that title in Brazil next weekend.

McLaren’s Oscar Piastri was seventh at the flag but ​was then handed a 10-second penalty for causing a collision and demoted to 15th.

That initially moved Franco Colapinto to seventh and his Alpine teammate Pierre Gasly to ninth, but both later lost their points when they were handed 10-second penalties for ‌going too fast ⁠under yellow flags.

The post-race penalties moved Racing Bulls’ Liam Lawson up to seventh, Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto to eighth, Red Bull’s Isack Hadjar to ninth, and allowed Ryo Hirakawa to score a point in 10th on his Haas debut.

The race was stopped, after a brief safety car deployment, on lap 46 of 71 after Valtteri Bottas suffered a high-speed front-left suspension failure down the straight with his Cadillac pitched uncontrollably into the barriers at turn one.

Bottas received medical attention in the car but then walked to an ambulance, giving a thumbs up, as the rest of the field returned to the pits. He went to the medical centre and was released.

Verstappen led from the restart, challenged ​by Hamilton with Antonelli passing Leclerc, and there was then ​another safety car when Lindblad and Piastri collided – ⁠with the field released to race again with nine laps to the chequered flag.

The four-time champion, cleared of a false start, hung on to take his 74th career win – and sixth in Mexico – by 0.799 of a second with Antonelli four seconds down the road.

Ferrari pair collide

Hamilton had led away from the original pole position, for the ​105th time in his career but first for Ferrari at a full Grand Prix, with Leclerc slotting in behind from third on the grid.

The Briton held him ​off as they went side by ⁠side through the opening corners but Leclerc cut turn four and went across the grass as they battled for the lead, with Verstappen then taking second from Hamilton as the Ferrari looped wide.

“Pushed out by my own teammate,” said Hamilton over the radio.

Stewards handed Leclerc a five-second penalty but that did little for Hamilton, who remained behind his teammate after their respective stops on laps 28 and 29 with the Monegasque taking his penalty.

“The problem with the five-second penalty is ⁠he’s got clean ​air and doesn’t have to manage like the rest of us. He should just give the positions back,” said the seven-time world ​champion.

Stewards said neither car would have made the corner on track, given the speed they were going.

Russell, who had lined up on the front row, made a poor start and dropped to fifth. The Briton also collided with Hadjar, with the Red Bull punted off, and the ​stewards handed him a 10-second penalty.

Hadjar pitted for a change of tyres when a virtual safety car was deployed on lap seven after Lance Stroll stopped his Aston Martin on track.

Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton started from pole position and took a close second place – after clashing with teammate Charles Leclerc – on an afternoon of drama with two safety cars, multiple crashes and an agonising 33-minute halt with 25 of the 71 laps remaining.

“We did it, thank you so much,” gasped the Italian, whose parents and sister were there to embrace him when he stepped out of the car. He was then mobbed by his pit crew.

The previous youngest champion was Germany’s Sebastian Vettel, who took the first of his four with Red Bull at 23 years and 134 days in 2010.

“I’m speechless. I’m trying to process what has just happened,” said Antonelli in comments to the crowd.

“It’s ⁠been an incredible season, and to share this podium with Max and Lewis is truly incredible. And looking forward to some more battles in the future.

“This weekend I did feel a bit more tense, but I’m just so happy that we got it done, and now we can enjoy the rest of the season,” he added, with an Italian flag wrapped around his shoulders on the podium and spraying the champagne with abandon.

The last Italian champion was Alberto Ascari, 73 years earlier.

“On the last lap, I just backed off because I just couldn’t see the track. I was getting emotional,” Antonelli told a later news conference.

“So it was just good to bring it home.”

Leclerc finished fourth, McLaren’s outgoing champion Lando Norris was fifth and Antonelli’s teammate George Russell only sixth in a race he had to win to have any chance of staying in contention.

That also meant Verstappen went second in the overall standings, with Hamilton third and pre-season favourite Russell plummeting to fourth and 130 points behind Antonelli.

Mercedes have 630 points in the constructors’ standings to Ferrari’s 504 and could clinch that title in Brazil next weekend.

McLaren’s Oscar Piastri was seventh at the flag but was then handed a 10-second penalty for causing a collision and demoted to 15th.

That initially moved Franco Colapinto to seventh and his Alpine teammate Pierre Gasly to ninth, but both later lost their points when they were handed 10-second penalties for ‌going too fast ⁠under yellow flags.

The post-race penalties moved Racing Bulls’ Liam Lawson up to seventh, Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto to eighth, Red Bull’s Isack Hadjar to ninth, and allowed Ryo Hirakawa to score a point in 10th on his Haas debut.

The race was stopped, after a brief safety car deployment, on lap 46 of 71 after Valtteri Bottas suffered a high-speed front-left suspension failure down the straight with his Cadillac pitched uncontrollably into the barriers at turn one.

Hamilton had led away from the original pole position, for the 105th time in his career but first for Ferrari at a full Grand Prix, with Leclerc slotting in behind from third on the grid.

“Pushed out by my own teammate,” said Hamilton over the radio.

Stewards handed Leclerc a five-second penalty but that did little for Hamilton, who remained behind his teammate after their respective stops on laps 28 and 29 with the Monegasque taking his penalty.

“The problem with the five-second penalty is ⁠he’s got clean air and doesn’t have to manage like the rest of us. He should just give the positions back,” said the seven-time world champion.

Stewards said neither car would have made the corner on track, given the speed they were going.

Russell, who had lined up on the front row, made a poor start and dropped to fifth. The Briton also collided with Hadjar, with the Red Bull punted off, and the stewards handed him a 10-second penalty.

headline: World's energy supply buffers eroded, ADNOC CEO says
description: ADNOC chief warns of shrinking oil reserves and growing supply risks
author: Reuters
article_text:
The world has eroded its supply buffers by draining nearly 1 billion oil barrels from global ​inventories since the US-Israeli war on Iran disrupted shipping ‌through the Strait of Hormuz, the CEO of Abu Dhabi’s state-owned oil company ADNOC said.

Diesel stockpiles in some areas are at 35-year lows ​for this time of the season, while others face an LNG supply gap of ​600 billion cubic feet, Sultan Al Jaber added on Monday at the ⁠UAE’s ADIPEC conference.

Prices of diesel in many markets have surged ​to record highs, boosted by wartime supply disruptions and pose inflation and cost-of-living ​threats to governments and consumers.

“We need expanded strategic storage, larger stockpiles of products, and flexible refining capacity closer to consumer markets,” Al Jaber said. “Infrastructure ​must be built before it is needed and enabled ​by advanced logistics.”

The cost of shipping and logistics has risen to 30% of the ‌cost ⁠of a barrel, from 5% before the Iran war, Al Jaber said.

The international benchmark Brent is trading around $110 a barrel, up about 50% from February just before the war began.

Last month, ​the International Energy ​Agency agreed ⁠to release more than 20 million barrels of diesel to the market and any oil remaining from a ​record emergency reserves release pledged in March ​to boost ⁠supply and cool soaring prices.

Amin Nasser, CEO of Saudi Arabia’s state oil company Saudi Aramco, said last month that fewer than 6 billion barrels ⁠of commercial ​inventories remained, with the vast majority not ​practically available.

headline: Israeli strikes kill three people in Gaza, medics say
description: Several others are wounded as attacks add to tensions over fragile ceasefire
author: Reuters
article_text:
Israeli strikes killed at least three Palestinians and wounded several others in the Gaza Strip on Monday, the ​territory’s health officials said.

Medics said two people were killed ‌and six others wounded in two separate airstrikes in Khan Younis, south of the enclave, while a third person was killed in an Israeli ​airstrike in the town of Al-Mussadar.

The Israeli military didn’t ​immediately comment on any of the attacks.

Israel, which says ⁠the Hamas militant group has been rearming and launching attacks ​in violation of a year-old ceasefire, has stepped up strikes on ​the group in recent weeks.

Hamas has denied trying to carry out attacks or rebuild its arsenal and accuses Israel of undermining the Gaza peace ​deal.

Last year’s US-brokered ceasefire calls for eventual reconstruction of the ​territory.

But little progress has been made as negotiators have failed to agree ‌on ⁠terms for Hamas to disarm or Israel to withdraw its troops, who control about two-thirds of the territory where they have ordered residents out.

Nearly all of the more than 2 million ​residents live in ​the remaining third ⁠of the enclave among war ruins, mostly in makeshift tents and damaged buildings, still under effective ​control of Hamas.

At least 1,580 Palestinians have been ​killed ⁠in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the ceasefire, according to the territory’s health officials, while Israel says four soldiers have been killed.

Palestinian ⁠authorities ​say more than 74,000 people have been ​killed in Israel’s assault on Gaza, launched after Hamas-led fighters killed about 1,200 ​people in southern Israel on October 7, 2023.

headline: Death toll in Sialkot stampede rises as injured man succumbs
description: Police register a case against TikToker Mr Patlo and more than 40 others; he goes into hiding
author: Web Desk
article_text:
The death toll from a stampede at the mehndi ceremony of TikToker Ansar Jutt, popularly known as Mr Patlo, in Sialkot has risen to two, while 12 others were injured, police said on Monday.

The incident occurred at a cricket stadium on Daska Road on Sunday, where a large number of people had gathered after the TikToker invited the public to attend the ceremony, with prizes also scheduled to be distributed through a lucky draw.

People from Sialkot and other cities across Punjab had arrived at the venue, but a stampede broke out before the event began, leaving 14 people injured.

One victim, identified as Aqeel, died, while another injured man, Rehan, was shifted to Lahore, where he later succumbed to his injuries.

The police have registered a case against more than 40 suspects, including Jutt, and arrested six people, while raids are being launched to arrest the TikToker.

Meanwhile, in a video statement, Jutt denied responsibility for the incident, saying he was at a hospital when the stampede occurred.

He claimed he had obtained a no-objection certificate (NOC) for the event but later cancelled it himself.

He also appealed to the government, including Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz, for help, citing his own ill health and his father’s deteriorating condition.

article_html:
The death toll from a stampede at the mehndi ceremony of TikToker Ansar Jutt, popularly known as Mr Patlo, in Sialkot has risen to two, while 12 others were injured, police said on Monday.

The incident occurred at a cricket stadium on Daska Road on Sunday, where a large number of people had gathered after the TikToker invited the public to attend the ceremony, with prizes also scheduled to be distributed through a lucky draw.

People from Sialkot and other cities across Punjab had arrived at the venue, but a stampede broke out before the event began, leaving 14 people injured.

One victim, identified as Aqeel, died, while another injured man, Rehan, was shifted to Lahore, where he later succumbed to his injuries.

The police have registered a case against more than 40 suspects, including Jutt, and arrested six people, while raids are being launched to arrest the TikToker.

Meanwhile, in a video statement, Jutt denied responsibility for the incident, saying he was at a hospital when the stampede occurred.

He claimed he had obtained a no-objection certificate (NOC) for the event but later cancelled it himself.

He also appealed to the government, including Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz, for help, citing his own ill health and his father’s deteriorating condition.

headline: Pakistan faces LPG crisis ahead of winter amid closure of Iran supply route
description: Falling gas supplies and rising LPG prices threaten households and small businesses
author: Ali Khizar
article_text:
With pipeline gas dwindling and LNG scarce, households and small eateries increasingly depend on LPG. Closing the Iran supply route before winter risks turning an energy shortage into a cooking-fuel crisis, according to Business Recorder.

Pakistan is heading into winter with less gas and too little preparation. Imported LNG is short, domestic pipeline supply is falling, and households and small businesses increasingly depend on liquefied petroleum gas for cooking. LPG supplies less than 5 percent of primary energy, but that understates its importance. A shortage may barely register in the national energy balance while causing considerable trouble in the kitchen.

The first problem is that nobody has a reliable measure of how much LPG the country consumes, or how many people depend on it. Official domestic production is around 2,200 tonnes a day. The balance comes from imports, some by sea, but much of it overland from Iran, through both formal trade and smuggling.

That land route has now been shut, without warning or an adequate replacement supply plan. Prices have jumped, and traders have little certainty about when supplies might resume. Closing a major source of cooking fuel just before peak demand was always going to have consequences. Consumers are beginning to discover them.

The petroleum ministry’s answer is to accelerate deregulation. The reform is overdue: a pricing regime that makes formal imports commercially unattractive leaves the market dependent on informal supply. But changing the rules will take time to bring additional cargoes, investment and competition. It is no substitute for securing fuel this winter.

The pricing problem is straightforward. Ogra set the October price at around Rs280 per kg, using Saudi free-on-board prices without adequately allowing for Pakistan-specific freight and insurance costs. Formal importers say they cannot bring in gas commercially at that price. Informal suppliers, some of whom also evade taxes, have consequently filled much of the gap.

The border closure has exposed this arrangement. Reported retail prices have climbed to Rs600–700 per kg, while the regulated domestic producer price remains around Rs280. The official price has become increasingly detached from what consumers actually pay.

The sums are substantial. Applied to domestic production of 2,200 tonnes a day, the reported difference between producer and retail prices implies a gross spread exceeding Rs700m daily, before transport, distribution and other costs. That is not a measure of net profit, and prices vary across markets. It is nevertheless a reason to examine who is capturing the scarcity premium.

A price ceiling that discourages replacement imports while failing to restrain retail prices offers consumers little protection. Domestic supply remains cheap at one end of the chain and expensive at the other. Somewhere between the two, the benefits of regulation disappear.

Government sources estimate winter demand at 6,000–7,000 tonnes a day. Informal traders put it closer to 10,000. Neither estimate inspires much confidence in a market with such weak visibility. LNG shortages could push more consumers towards cylinders, making it especially risky to plan around the lower figure.

The Sui gas companies intend to divert gas from power generation to households. That may ease pressure on cooking fuel, but it shifts the shortage elsewhere. Depending on replacement generation and fuel availability, the result could be more expensive electricity or additional load-shedding. Buying spot LNG would also carry a cost. There is no painless rearrangement of an inadequate fuel supply.

The damage extends beyond household budgets. Small restaurants, roadside eateries and food vendors rely heavily on LPG. Higher fuel costs squeeze their margins and feed into meal prices. Interrupted supplies reduce operating hours and threaten employment. Households without pipeline gas face a more basic problem: having food is of limited comfort when cooking it becomes unaffordable.

These consumers have fewer ways to absorb the shock. A large hotel can invest in alternative equipment and negotiate supply arrangements. A small eatery or a household buying cylinders has much less room to manoeuvre.

The government should also review how its fuel levies interact with the shortage. Where furnace oil or diesel must replace gas in power generation, taxation adds to an already expensive adjustment. Any temporary relief would need to be assessed against its fiscal cost and passed through to consumers. But maintaining every levy unchanged while fuel availability deteriorates is hardly a coherent energy response.

The finance minister’s emphasis on basic macroeconomic hygiene has its place. It does not answer the immediate question of how households will cook this winter. An economy can meet its fiscal targets while making daily life substantially harder for people whose hardship is poorly captured by the headline numbers.

The immediate task is to restore predictable LPG supplies. Islamabad should reopen a workable, monitored trade route with Iran and facilitate replacement imports by sea. It should investigate withholding, collusion and excessive intermediation margins, with recovery or taxation of identifiable windfalls where the evidence supports it. Announcing a windfall tax is easier than collecting one from an opaque supply chain.

Deregulation should proceed alongside better reporting of imports, stocks and retail prices. Formal suppliers need a commercially workable route into the market, and consumers need competition that reaches the cylinder.

The macroeconomic cost of a cooking-gas shortage may look modest. The human cost will not. Islamabad has had ample warning that pipeline supply is declining and LPG dependence is growing. A winter shortage compounded by its own supply decisions would be a policy failure.

Government sources estimate winter demand at 6,000–7,000 tonnes a day. Informal traders put it closer to 10,000. Neither estimate inspires much confidence in a market with such weak visibility. LNG shortages could push more consumers towards cylinders, making it especially risky to plan around the lower figure.

The Sui gas companies intend to divert gas from power generation to households. That may ease pressure on cooking fuel, but it shifts the shortage elsewhere. Depending on replacement generation and fuel availability, the result could be more expensive electricity or additional load-shedding. Buying spot LNG would also carry a cost. There is no painless rearrangement of an inadequate fuel supply.

The damage extends beyond household budgets. Small restaurants, roadside eateries and food vendors rely heavily on LPG. Higher fuel costs squeeze their margins and feed into meal prices. Interrupted supplies reduce operating hours and threaten employment. Households without pipeline gas face a more basic problem: having food is of limited comfort when cooking it becomes unaffordable.

These consumers have fewer ways to absorb the shock. A large hotel can invest in alternative equipment and negotiate supply arrangements. A small eatery or a household buying cylinders has much less room to manoeuvre.

The government should also review how its fuel levies interact with the shortage. Where furnace oil or diesel must replace gas in power generation, taxation adds to an already expensive adjustment. Any temporary relief would need to be assessed against its fiscal cost and passed through to consumers. But maintaining every levy unchanged while fuel availability deteriorates is hardly a coherent energy response.

The finance minister’s emphasis on basic macroeconomic hygiene has its place. It does not answer the immediate question of how households will cook this winter. An economy can meet its fiscal targets while making daily life substantially harder for people whose hardship is poorly captured by the headline numbers.

The immediate task is to restore predictable LPG supplies. Islamabad should reopen a workable, monitored trade route with Iran and facilitate replacement imports by sea. It should investigate withholding, collusion and excessive intermediation margins, with recovery or taxation of identifiable windfalls where the evidence supports it. Announcing a windfall tax is easier than collecting one from an opaque supply chain.

Deregulation should proceed alongside better reporting of imports, stocks and retail prices. Formal suppliers need a commercially workable route into the market, and consumers need competition that reaches the cylinder.

The macroeconomic cost of a cooking-gas shortage may look modest. The human cost will not. Islamabad has had ample warning that pipeline supply is declining and LPG dependence is growing. A winter shortage compounded by its own supply decisions would be a policy failure.

headline: ICC fines Pakistan 5% of match fee for slow over-rate in ODI final
description: Shaheen Afridi admits offence after Pakistan fall one over short against Sri Lanka in Lahore
article_text:
The International Cricket Council (ICC) has fined Pakistan’s cricket team 5% of its match fee for maintaining a slow over rate in the recently held final of the three-nation ODI series against Sri Lanka in Lahore.

According to the ICC, Pakistan were one over short of the required rate within the stipulated time.

Captain Shaheen Shah Afridi admitted the offence and accepted the proposed sanction.

Pakistan won the final by three wickets after chasing down Sri Lanka’s target of 326 runs.

headline: Ukraine says public air raid alert app sent false alerts after being hacked
description: False alerts appeared in Kyiv and other areas before app was taken offline
author: Reuters
article_text:
Ukraine’s Air Force said on Sunday that the public ​air raid alert app had been ‌hacked.

The app for a short time showed Kyiv and other areas subject to nuclear and chemical ​alerts and the threat of street ​combat. An erroneous message said Russia’s hypersonic ⁠Oreshnik missile had been deployed.

“The air ​alert app appears to have been subjected to ​enemy influence,” the air force said on Telegram. “There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our ​updates on our channel!”

The abnormality later ​disappeared.

Ukraine’s Ministry for Digital Transformation said the app was ‌not ⁠in operation, but other means of alerting the public were functioning, as were air raid sirens.

In a separate event, the mobile ​app of Russia’s ​emergencies ⁠ministry was hit by a massive cyberattack that resulted in the ​spread of false information to the ​public, ⁠state news agency TASS quoted the ministry as saying early on Monday.

It was not ⁠immediately clear ​whether the two incidents ​were linked.

headline: Bangladesh garment factories reopen amid wage unrest
description: Manufacturers warn of more disruption as workers demand minimum wage of 30,000 taka
author: Reuters
article_text:
Bangladesh’s garment factories reopened on Monday after widespread closures and production disruptions a day earlier, but manufacturers remain concerned about further unrest over workers’ demands for higher wages.

The ready-made garment sector accounts for more than 80% of Bangladesh’s export earnings, employs about 4 million workers and contributes around 10% to ​gross domestic product.

The latest unrest disrupted operations in key manufacturing hubs and raised concerns over export ​shipments and buyer confidence in Bangladesh, the world’s second-largest apparel exporter after China, as ⁠workers demanded a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka ($243), up from 12,500 taka.

The demand reflects mounting pressure ​from rising living costs and persistent inflation.

The government formed a six-member minimum wage board on Sunday to review ​the demand, but the move failed to immediately quell unrest.

Workers set up road blockades in several industrial areas on Sunday, with police in the capital Dhaka using tear gas and water cannons to disperse protesters.

“Bangladesh has among the lowest garment wages ​in the world,” said Babul Akhter, general secretary of the Bangladesh Garment and Industrial Workers Federation and ​a workers’ representative on the wage board.

“If factory owners cannot pay workers properly, they should negotiate better prices with international ‌buyers. They ⁠cannot build a business on the backs of underpaid workers.”

No work, no pay

Factory owners said the industry faces higher costs, energy market uncertainty linked to conflict in the Middle East and slowing demand in key export markets.

The Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) said demonstrations in multiple cities disrupted operations at 529 factories and ​affected nearly 1 million ​workers.

“The government has already ⁠taken a step by forming the wage board. We expect workers to allow the review process to proceed,” said BGMEA President Mahmud Hasan Khan.

“If protests break out ​later in the day and we are forced to shut factories, we will ​have no option ⁠but to invoke the ‘no work, no pay’ provision,” he said, adding that industry representatives were scheduled to meet the home minister to discuss the unrest.

Selim Raihan, an economics professor at the University of Dhaka, said workers’ demands were ⁠understandable given ​high inflation, and suppressed wages could cause further unrest.

However, he ​cautioned that a substantial wage increase could raise production costs, squeeze exporters’ profit margins and weaken Bangladesh’s price competitiveness.

“A phased wage adjustment, improved ​productivity and fairer pricing from international buyers are essential to balancing workers’ welfare with industrial sustainability.”

headline: Pakistan, China set to deepen strategic ties during senior CPC official's visit
description: Liu Haixing's visit aims to strengthen Pakistan-China cooperation
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Pakistan is hosting a senior Chinese Communist Party official on Monday for talks aimed at strengthening bilateral cooperation, as the two countries seek to expand their longstanding strategic partnership.

Liu Haixing, Minister of the International Department of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee, is visiting Pakistan for the first time on an official invitation from Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar.

According to Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry, Liu will meet the country’s leadership and co-chair a high-level event with Dar in Islamabad.

“The visit forms part of the ongoing high-level and party-to-party exchanges between Pakistan and China, reflecting the two countries’ shared commitment to further strengthening their All-Weather Strategic Cooperative Partnership,” the ministry said.

China is Pakistan’s largest trading partner and a key strategic ally. Both countries maintain close cooperation in trade, defence, infrastructure and regional security.

The visit comes days after Pakistan and China established an 18-outlet news exchange network and a dedicated fact-checking mechanism under a newly launched information corridor, Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said.

The corridor’s business component has also opened its first regional office in Karachi. Its think-tank component, led by the Pakistan-China Institute, will connect research institutions from both countries for joint discussions, research and publications.

China has pledged more than $65 billion in investment in Pakistan through road, infrastructure and development projects under the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC).

Several Chinese private-sector manufacturers have also entered joint ventures in Pakistan.

The International Department of the CPC Central Committee manages the party’s relations with political parties and organisations worldwide and conducts foreign exchanges to support China’s international engagement.

Liu Haixing, Minister of the International Department of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee, is visiting Pakistan for the first time on an official invitation from Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar.

According to Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry, Liu will meet the country’s leadership and co-chair a high-level event with Dar in Islamabad.

“The visit forms part of the ongoing high-level and party-to-party exchanges between Pakistan and China, reflecting the two countries’ shared commitment to further strengthening their All-Weather Strategic Cooperative Partnership,” the ministry said.

China is Pakistan’s largest trading partner and a key strategic ally. Both countries maintain close cooperation in trade, defence, infrastructure and regional security.

The visit comes days after Pakistan and China established an 18-outlet news exchange network and a dedicated fact-checking mechanism under a newly launched information corridor, Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said.

The corridor’s business component has also opened its first regional office in Karachi. Its think-tank component, led by the Pakistan-China Institute, will connect research institutions from both countries for joint discussions, research and publications.

China has pledged more than $65 billion in investment in Pakistan through road, infrastructure and development projects under the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC).

Several Chinese private-sector manufacturers have also entered joint ventures in Pakistan.

The International Department of the CPC Central Committee manages the party’s relations with political parties and organisations worldwide and conducts foreign exchanges to support China’s international engagement.

headline: China's 'Hollywood' turns visitors into stars with immersive drama experience
description: Tourists are paying to dress up and film their own historical dramas at Hengdian Studios
author: Reuters
article_text:
Onlookers ‌craned their necks outside an ornate palace chamber, peering through the doors at four women in silk robes and jade hairpins acting out a court intrigue.

One consort slapped another across the face, the director called for another take, and the cast huddled over ​their phones. Then they started laughing.

But the scene was not for a television drama.

The women were friends who ​had travelled more than 1,500 km to star in their own production at ⁠Hengdian World Studios, the sprawling complex in eastern China known as “China’s Hollywood”, where many of the country’s period dramas ​are filmed.

The studio has expanded into experiential tourism, allowing visitors to shoot their own scenes on sets ranging from ​a replica of Beijing’s Forbidden City to old Shanghai streets used in professional productions.

Since the experience launched in August, Hengdian said more than 2,000 people had taken part, with bookings full on most days, particularly during weekends and holidays.

“During the National Day holiday, I ​shoot from morning until dark, and there are still guests we can’t fit in,” said Wang Weili, a ​director who once filmed 20 groups in a single day.

The attraction reflects a broader shift in Chinese consumer spending.

While a slowing economy and ‌prolonged ⁠property slump have weighed on purchases of everything from luxury goods to home furnishings, consumers have continued to spend on travel, entertainment and experiences, fuelling demand for immersive attractions such as live-action role-playing games, historical re-enactments and interactive film shoots.

“When I was a kid, I loved playing director and getting the other children to act out scenes,” said ​Clare Huang, who was ​playing an empress in her ⁠group’s palace drama.

“I’ve always enjoyed this kind of thing, so today a few of us girls get to see what it feels like.”

For 388 yuan ($55) each, Huang and ​her friends got their hair and makeup done, costumes, a 30-minute directed shoot and a ​90-second edited video. ⁠Guests can choose from more than 20 scripts, most involving palace intrigue, romance or betrayal.

Another customer, Xie, a 28-year-old influencer who gave only her family name, travelled to Hengdian after seeing videos of the shoots on social media. She paid 498 ⁠yuan ($70) ​for a solo session based on an original script.

“We don’t have proms ​in China, so now people go out in costume instead,” Xie said. “Everyone is willing to dress up a bit more boldly and show themselves ​in the best way they can.”

headline: Netanyahu pressing Trump for Iran nuclear attack: Report
description: US commentator Tucker Carlson says Netanyahu is trying to protect his political future
author: Web Desk
article_text:
US political commentator Tucker Carlson has claimed that President Donald Trump could be days away from authorising a nuclear strike on Iran, alleging that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is pressing Washington to attack a suspected nuclear site in central Iran.

In a post on X late Sunday, Carlson identified the potential target as Pickaxe Mountain, where Israeli intelligence believes Iran has resumed its nuclear enrichment programme.

He claimed conventional US weapons could not penetrate the estimated 300 feet of solid granite protecting underground tunnels at the site, leaving a nuclear strike as the only military option.

“Bibi (Netanyahu) calls Trump about it every day,” Carlson quoted an unnamed source as saying.

Carlson alleged that Netanyahu was seeking renewed military action to protect his political future, claiming the Israeli prime minister needed Trump’s support to secure a 61-seat majority in the Knesset and avoid losing power, facing investigations and possible imprisonment.

He further claimed Netanyahu had been pressing senior US officials, including Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and Central Command chief Admiral Brad Cooper, to resume major combat operations.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio and CIA Director John Ratcliffe were also allegedly following Netanyahu’s lead, he said.

Carlson warned that renewed fighting could have severe regional and global consequences, saying eight months of conflict had already hurt Gulf economies and disrupted energy and fertiliser markets.

He also claimed 11 of the world’s approximately 850 oil supertankers were badly damaged in the Strait of Hormuz in October.

He warned that a nuclear explosion at Pickaxe Mountain could contaminate the Gulf and threaten the water supply of around 100 million people.

Carlson alleged that the Trump administration had quietly revised US nuclear doctrine since February to make the first use of so-called battlefield nuclear weapons easier.

He said Trump could decide by November 7 whether to authorise their use.

Vance, Witkoff favour diplomacy

Carlson claimed Vice President JD Vance and US special envoy Steve Witkoff were urging Trump to pursue a diplomatic agreement with Tehran rather than resume military action.

He said people who had spoken with Iranian decision-makers believed there was a consensus that further conflict would benefit no one and that an agreement was worth pursuing.

He also alleged that Netanyahu had secretly travelled to Abu Dhabi on September 27 to seek UAE support for a final attack on Iran, but Emirati officials had refused.

Carlson further claimed former US president Barack Obama opposed the Iran peace agreement being drafted in Doha.

Trump says sites could be struck within minutes

Carlson’s claims followed Trump’s remarks at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida on Saturday that one or two Iranian nuclear facilities remained potential targets and could be struck within 10 minutes.

Trump specifically mentioned Pickaxe Mountain, saying the US had military plans for the area, but did not indicate that a nuclear strike had been authorised.
